Confido raised a $55 million Series B led by Insight Partners to expand its AI platform for finance, accounting, sales planning and supply chain work across consumer packaged goods companies. More than 250 brands now use the platform to manage over $30 billion in retail sales planning.

Confido raised $55 million in a Series B round to expand its AI platform for consumer packaged goods companies, giving the New York startup $77 million in total funding.

Insight Partners led the round. Trenches Capital, Watchfire, Barrel Ventures, Footwork and Y Combinator also participated. Confido plans to invest the capital in product development, AI workflows and hiring.

The company sells software that connects finance, accounting, sales and operations on one system. Its tools help brands resolve retail deductions, track trade spending, improve forecasts and coordinate supply chain decisions. Confido says its platform surfaces exceptions and decisions for employees instead of asking teams to review every transaction by hand.

More than 250 brands use Confido, including Daisy, Dude Wipes, Kettle & Fire, Unilever and Mars. Those customers route more than $30 billion in retail sales planning through the platform. Confido says revenue and usage have grown fivefold year over year since its Series A.

Consumer packaged goods companies manage thousands of products across retailers, distributors and sales channels. Each transaction can create deductions, promotional costs, inventory changes or forecasting updates that affect a brand’s margin.

Many companies still manage those tasks through spreadsheets, disconnected enterprise systems, outside consultants and manual business-process work. Finance teams often discover errors during month-end close, after a company has lost the chance to correct a shipment, dispute a charge or adjust a promotion.

Confido targets that gap with software built for CPG workflows. The platform connects commercial data with financial and operational records, giving teams a shared view of sales plans, retailer activity, trade spend and forecasts.

The company estimates that the global CPG industry represents about $2.5 trillion in annual economic activity. It also estimates that companies spend more than $100 billion each year on software and services that support the sector.

That spending creates room for vendors that can replace manual work with systems that execute tasks. Confido competes for that opportunity with enterprise resource planning software, trade promotion management tools, revenue management products and specialized finance systems.

Many business software products use AI to summarize information, generate reports or answer questions. Confido is building AI agents that can carry out work across finance, accounting, forecasting and sales planning.

A deduction workflow, for example, can identify a retailer charge, compare it with shipment and promotion records, assemble supporting documents and route the case for approval. A forecasting workflow can combine sales history, retailer plans and operational data before presenting a proposed update to a planner.

Human employees still handle decisions that require judgment. The software takes responsibility for the repetitive steps that consume time across large transaction volumes.

Confido co-founder and CEO Justin Hunter said his family gave him an early connection to the sector. His mother managed retail stores for Target, and his father sold software to consumer brands. Hunter later worked with consumer companies and saw finance and operations teams rely on manual processes despite the scale of their businesses.

The company built its product around CPG-specific data and workflows instead of adapting a general-purpose back-office tool. That focus includes retailer deductions, trade promotion activity, forecasting and supply chain planning.

Confido sells its products through annual subscriptions. Customers can buy individual modules, though the company says many adopt more than one because the products share data.

That model gives Confido a path to expand within each customer. A brand that starts with deduction management can add trade spend, forecasting or broader financial workflows. Each additional product can increase the value of the shared dataset and raise the cost of replacing the platform.

The strategy also creates execution risks. Confido must maintain accurate integrations with retailers, finance systems and operational tools. Its AI agents must produce reliable work across high-value transactions, where an incorrect deduction decision or forecast can affect cash flow and inventory.

Customer retention will provide a key test. Growth across 250 brands gives the company scale, but long-term adoption will depend on measurable improvements in margin, forecasting accuracy and staff productivity.

Confido plans to use the new capital to launch more agent-driven workflows and extend coverage across the commercial cycle. The company also expects to grow its team as demand increases.

Hunter has described the long-term goal as an operating system for the back office of consumer brands. Reaching that goal would require Confido to connect more departments, data sources and decisions than a single finance product can handle.

Economic pressure could support that expansion. Brands with tight margins need better control over trade spending, deductions, inventory and forecasts when sales slow or costs rise. Software that helps employees find errors before month-end close can compete for budget even when companies reduce other technology spending.

For startups without new funding, Hunter’s advice is direct: focus on profitability and customer growth. Confido now has capital to pursue a larger product vision, but the company still needs to show that AI can deliver durable financial results for the brands using its platform.

Confido’s website provides more information about the company’s platform and products.

HIFI raises $37 million to scale tokenized capital-markets infrastructure HIFI raised $37 million in a Series A led by Left Lane Capital as demand grows for stablecoin payments and blockchain-based securities settlement. The company plans to expand its API platform, which connects bank rails, digital assets, compliance and settlement across 87 countries.

Numeral's $100m Series C bets on sales tax complexity Numeral raised $100 million in a Series C led by Insight Partners as companies face expanding sales tax rules across states, countries and product categories. The compliance platform will use the funding to expand its tax engine, enter new industries and hire across product, engineering, sales and marketing.

Unspin turns fake-news detection into a game Unspin presents fact-checking as a fast quiz built around strange claims, familiar myths and misleading headlines. Its concept has promise, but the supplied description leaves key questions about evidence, scoring and educational depth unanswered.
